content: This publication is an updated version of the Guidelines for Poison Control, originally published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 1997. The update reflects advancements in the roles and activities of poison centres, as well as developments in information technology and communication. It also emphasizes the critical role of poison centres in public health, particularly following the revision of the International Health Regulations (IHR) in 2005, which require countries to have the capacity for surveillance, detection, and response to public health events caused by chemicals. The guidelines provide detailed instructions for establishing and strengthening poison centres, which are specialized units that assist in the prevention, diagnosis, and management of poisoning. Poison centres play a vital role in addressing the global public health problem of poisoning, which is responsible for significant morbidity and mortality worldwide. For example, poisoning accounts for millions of disability-adjusted life years lost annually and is a major cause of emergency hospital visits in many countries. The document outlines the history of poison centres, their policy background, and the services they offer. It provides practical guidance on setting up poisons information services, clinical toxicology services, and analytical toxicology services. It also discusses the role of poison centres in toxicovigilance, the prevention of poisoning, and preparedness for chemical incidents. Additionally, the guidelines address issues related to antidote availability, data collection, staff training, quality assurance, and potential funding sources. The update was developed through a collaborative process involving experts in poison centres, medical toxicology, and analytical toxicology from all WHO regions. Contributions were made by the WHO Collaborating Centre for the Public Health Management of Chemical Exposures, the National Poisons Information Service (NPIS) units in the United Kingdom, and other international experts. The document underwent multiple rounds of review and revision to ensure its accuracy and relevance. The guidelines also highlight the importance of poison centres in supporting the sound management of chemicals and their integration into public health systems. They provide a framework for countries to establish or strengthen poison centres, addressing gaps in capacity for managing chemical exposures and improving public health outcomes.
